summary.text: The main sequence is the continuous, distinctive band that stars form on plots of stellar color versus brightness.
Stars spend the majority of their lives there, mainly burning hydrogen in their cores, and the Sun is one of them.
A star's place on the band is set mainly by its mass, and the more massive a star is, the shorter its time there.

facts.label: Other name
facts.value: Main-sequence stars are sometimes called dwarf stars

facts.label: Core fuel
facts.value: Hydrogen is fused into helium in the core

facts.label: Sun's hydrogen
facts.value: 74.9% of the Sun's mass is hydrogen

facts.label: Who named it
facts.value: Ejnar Hertzsprung named it after plotting star clusters

facts.label: Fully convective
facts.value: Stars below 0.4 solar masses undergo convection throughout

items.prompt: A huge star and a small star begin burning hydrogen in their cores at the same moment. Which one leaves the main sequence first?

options.label: The small star, since it has less fuel
The huge star, since it is more massive
Both leave at the same moment
Neither leaves; all stars stay on it forever

items.explain: The more massive a star is, the shorter its lifespan on the main sequence.

items.prompt: Gravity keeps trying to squeeze a main-sequence star inward. What holds it up?

options.label: A shell of cold gas pressing in from outside
The star spinning too fast to collapse
The pull of nearby stars
A pressure gradient from the heat of core fusion

items.explain: Thermal energy from fusion radiates out from the hot core, creating a strong pressure gradient that counters collapse and keeps the star in hydrostatic equilibrium.

items.prompt: Two stars sit at very different spots on the main sequence. What mostly accounts for the difference?

options.label: Mostly the difference in their mass
Mostly the difference in their distance from us
Mostly the difference in their rotation
Mostly the difference in their names

items.explain: Position on the main sequence is determined primarily by mass, and also by age and chemical composition.

items.prompt: Two stars have similar mass, but one has a much larger share of elements heavier than helium. What should you expect about its time on the main sequence?

options.label: Longer, because its core stays cool
The same, because only mass matters
Shorter, because its hotter core speeds up fusion
Longer, because its fuel is richer

items.explain: Higher metallicity raises opacity, so energy stays concentrated in the core; the hotter environment speeds fusion and shortens the time on the main sequence.

items.prompt: In 1906 Hertzsprung noticed that the reddest stars split into two groups. What set the groups apart?

options.label: One group was hotter than the other
One group was far brighter than the Sun and the other far fainter
One group was far closer than the other
One group was a different colour from the other

items.explain: Those stars were either much brighter than the Sun or much fainter, so he called them giants and dwarfs.

items.prompt: A main-sequence star has about three times the Sun's mass. How does its main way of making helium differ from the Sun's?

options.label: It mainly uses carbon, nitrogen and oxygen as intermediaries
It fuses helium rather than hydrogen
It uses the proton–proton chain even more heavily
It makes energy without any nuclear fusion

items.explain: Above about 1.5 solar masses, the CNO cycle dominates, while the Sun fuses hydrogen mainly by the proton–proton chain.
